title: From answers to action: Why the real measure of member experience is resolution
summary: Explore how a smarter benefits member experience goes beyond providing information to deliver personalized guidance.
body_markdown:
### Share


When a member logs in to check a balance, understand a claim or figure out how to use a benefit, finding the answer is only part of the experience. They still need to know what it means and what to do next.


For years, digital member experiences have focused on making information easier to access. And that matters. But as digital tools become more intelligent and personalized, expectations are changing. Members need more than an account summary or a helpful response. They need guidance that helps them move forward.


For the industry, that raises a more important question: Are we helping members find answers, or helping them get things done?


## Finding the answer is only the first step


Most member questions have a task behind them.


A member checking a balance may be deciding whether to use their account for an upcoming expense. Someone reviewing a claim may be trying to understand why it was denied and what they need to do next. A member looking into their benefits may be trying to make a decision with real financial implications.


In each case, the information matters. But the member’s need does not end when the information appears on the screen.


They still have to interpret it, connect it to their situation and determine their next move. If that means navigating to another part of the experience, searching for additional guidance or contacting support, the work is not finished.


Answering the question is useful. Helping the member resolve it is what makes the experience work.


## The account summary was never the whole experience


Digital self-service has made it easier for members to access balances, statements, transactions and claim details on their own time. These capabilities give members greater visibility into their accounts without requiring them to pick up the phone or wait for assistance.


But access and action are not the same thing.


An account summary can tell a member what happened. It may not help them understand why it happened, what their options are or how to address the issue. The information can be accurate and easy to find, yet the member may still be left to figure out the next step.


That gap becomes especially important when members are trying to solve a problem in the middle of a busy day. They do not necessarily want another place to look or another resource to consult. They want to make progress on the task that brought them there.


The opportunity is to move beyond presenting information and build experiences that help members use it.


## Smarter answers need to connect to the task


The category is already moving in this direction. Assistants, personalization and more intelligent guidance are changing how members interact with digital experiences. The question is no longer simply whether an experience can answer a question or help initiate an action.


The difference is how well that guidance connects to what the member is actually trying to accomplish.


An assistant can provide a useful explanation or recommend a next step. But if the member still has to connect that advice to their account, locate the relevant claim or work out how to act on the guidance, there is still friction in the experience.


Guidance becomes more valuable when it is part of the task itself: informed by the member’s real account and claim information, relevant to their situation and connected to the next steps they need to take.


That connection matters. A more personalized answer does not automatically mean a simpler experience. And a more intelligent interaction does not necessarily mean the member has reached a resolution.


The real opportunity is to bring information, guidance and action closer together, so members can move from understanding their situation to doing something about it.


## The standard is getting to done


This changes how we should evaluate member experience.


The question is not simply whether an assistant can answer accurately, whether information is easy to find or whether the interaction feels personalized. Those capabilities matter, but they are part of the foundation.


The more important question is whether the experience helps the member complete the task.


Can they understand what is happening and what to do next? Can they act on guidance without unnecessary navigation or effort? Does the experience help resolve the need that brought them there in the first place?


As expectations continue to evolve, the experiences that stand out will be the ones that make it easier for members to move from information to action. Not simply showing members what they need to know, but helping them put that knowledge to work.


Because the best member experience isn’t the one that gives the best answer. It’s the one that helps members get where they need to go.
